title: Feature flag rollout guide (v1 to v2 update)
scenario: Source update and reconciliation: a rollout guide is revised. Between v1 and v2 one concept is unchanged, one explanation is reworded with one changed number, one concept is new, one is removed, one dependency gains a second condition, and the user has edited a card on the v1 canvas whose text must survive. One sentence is split in two (an ambiguous match).
objective: Keep a canvas made from v1 in step with v2 by changing only what changed, and never overwrite the user's own edit.

units.quote: This guide is for engineers who own a feature flag in the Orbit platform.
It explains how a flag goes from off to fully on, and what has to be true before each step.
It does not cover experiments, which follow their own process.
Each section below names the condition that must hold before the flag moves on.
Questions about the guide go to the platform team.
A rollout moves through three stages: internal, canary and general availability.
In the internal stage the flag is on only for staff accounts, so problems reach colleagues before they reach customers.
The internal stage usually lasts one working day, but the guide sets no minimum for it.
Canary then exposes a small share of real traffic to the change.
General availability turns the flag on for everyone, in steps of 25%, 50% and 100%.
Each stage is recorded in the rollout tool, which keeps the history of who moved the flag and when.
During canary the flag is on for 5% of requests, chosen at random per request rather than per user.
It must stay at that level for at least 30 minutes, so that the metrics cover a full traffic cycle of the slowest endpoint.
The owner does not raise the percentage by hand during this time, because a manual change restarts the measurement window.
Short canaries are the most common reason a bad flag reaches general availability.
A flag advances from canary to general availability only when the automated metrics check passes.

critical.note: The gate out of canary (v1: metrics check only).

units.quote: The metrics check compares the error rate and p95 latency of flagged requests with the same requests over the previous 7 days.
If the check fails, the flag stays in canary and the owner investigates before trying again.
The rollout tool runs the check automatically at the end of the canary window.
Every flag must have a kill switch that turns it off within 1 minute.

critical.note: The kill-switch requirement and its bound.

units.quote: The kill switch is tested in staging before the flag enters canary, and the test is recorded in the rollout tool.
A flag without a tested kill switch cannot enter canary.

critical.note: Canary depends on a tested kill switch.

units.quote: Anyone on the owning team may use the kill switch without asking for approval.
Turning a flag off is always safe; turning it back on starts the rollout again from the internal stage.
While the flag ramps up, the owner watches the error dashboard and pages the on-call engineer if errors rise.
The dashboard shows flagged and unflagged requests side by side, so a difference between them points at the flag rather than at the platform.
The owner keeps watching until the flag has been at 100% for one hour.
A flag that has been fully on for 30 days is removed from the code.
The owner opens a cleanup ticket when the flag reaches 100%, and the ticket links to the rollout record.
Flags that miss the deadline are listed in the weekly stale-flag report.
Old flags make the code harder to read and slow down every later rollout.

It explains how a flag goes from off to fully on, and what has to be true before each step.

Each stage is recorded in the rollout tool, which keeps the history of who moved the flag and when.
In the canary stage, 5% of requests see the flag, picked at random for each request instead of for each user.
The flag has to remain at 5% for no less than 60 minutes, so the metrics span a complete traffic cycle of the slowest endpoint.

critical.note: The minimum canary duration, changed from 30 to 60 minutes in v2.

units.quote: Owners leave the percentage alone during this window, since any manual change restarts the measurement.
Most bad flags that reach general availability got there through a canary that was too short.
A flag advances from canary to general availability only when the automated metrics check passes and the on-call engineer approves the move in the rollout tool.

critical.note: The gate out of canary now has two conditions: the metrics check and on-call approval.

units.quote: The metrics check compares the error rate and p95 latency of flagged requests with the same requests over the previous 7 days.
If the check fails, the flag stays in canary and the owner investigates before trying again.
The on-call engineer may decline the move while an incident is open, even when the check passes.
The rollout tool runs the check automatically at the end of the canary window.
Every flag must have a kill switch that turns it off within 1 minute.

ambiguity.note: v1's single sentence (u25) is split in two in v2 (u57, u58): no hash match and two partial candidates, so a unit matcher must call the lineage ambiguous.

units.quote: If errors rise, the owner pages the on-call engineer.

ambiguity.note: Second half of the split v1 sentence u25.

units.quote: The dashboard shows flagged and unflagged requests side by side, so a difference between them points at the flag rather than at the platform.
The owner keeps watching until the flag has been at 100% for one hour.
Before general availability, the owner rehearses a rollback once in staging: switch the flag off, confirm that the old behaviour returns, and switch it on again.
The rehearsal is recorded in the rollout tool next to the staging test.
It takes about 10 minutes and needs no approval.

provenance.note: Original text written for this dataset. The Orbit platform, the rollout tool, every percentage and duration, and the runbook id in the user's edit (RB-12) are invented. v2 is a deliberate revision of v1 written to exercise reconciliation.

review.notes: Model review 2026-10-19 (not a human review; needs a person before approval). All 63 quotes occur in their version; the v1 critical units (u13, u16, u20, u22) and their v2 counterparts (u44, u47, u52, u54) are marked alike; no v1 unit is marked superseded, which is right: accounting is per version and 30 → 60 minutes is lineage (reconcile.json), not a superseded statement within one version. Reconcile items checked against the v1/v2 diff and the user edit: change kinds, states and unitsBefore/unitsAfter are right (stages identical; canary reworded with 30 → 60; the gate gains on-call approval and u50; kill switch identical plus the user's edit; monitoring's u25 split into u57 + u58; cleanup removed; rehearsal added). The reference reconcile is faithful ('no less than 60 minutes', both gate conditions, the whole user note). Changed: (1) reconcile: i.kill-switch mustKeep now needs the whole user note ('during an incident use the Orbit console toggle, not the API'), not only 'Runbook RB-12': a truncated note passed. (2) evaluation: a.no-v2-in-v1 caught 'on-call approves' but not 'the on-call engineer must approve' or 'approval from on-call'; it now matches on-call and approv/sign within one clause in either order, and '60 min'; raised to critical (on the v1 canvas it changes the critical u13 / u16). New critical a.kill-switch-canary-condition (u22: a flag without a tested kill switch cannot enter canary; 'tested in staging before canary' alone doesn't say canary is blocked). a.rel-kill-switch raised to critical (it is u22's dependency). (3) case / knowledge: protected numbers added where a numeric unit had none (u8/u39 'one working day', u27/u60 'one hour', u29 '100%', u63 '10 minutes'); exactDetails completed (ku.stages 'one working day', ku.advance-gate 'p95', ku.ga-monitoring '100%' and 'one hour', ku.cleanup '100%'). Follow-up: regressions rg-12-approval-leaks-into-v1, rg-12-kill-switch-condition-dropped, rg-12-kill-switch-dependency-reversed and rg-12-user-note-truncated added. Open findings: i.canary is 'edited' + update_clean, which holds for section-level reconcile; under the §3.1 matcher every canary sentence is reworded below 0.8 word overlap, so card-level lineage would call u12–u15 removed and u43–u46 new and propose remove + add (a person should decide what card-level reconcile must do for a fully reworded section); reconcile checks can only require literal mustKeep strings, so i.canary doesn't require 'at least / no less than' (a fixed '60 minutes' passes) and i.advance-gate doesn't catch 'metrics check OR on-call approval' or a dropped 'only'; u57/u58 carry ambiguity for lineage reasons and the derived review_flagged check is not version-aware, so a v1 run checked with it would expect v2 units in Needs review; u14 (a manual change restarts the window), u18 (a failed check keeps the flag in canary), u25/u58 (page on-call if errors rise) and u50 (on-call may decline during an incident) are conditions left non-critical; e.canary matches '5%' + 'minute', which another card with both would also satisfy. Authoring note: v2 units get new ids (u32-u63) even where the sentence is unchanged; the lineage is recorded in reconcile.json (unitsBefore / unitsAfter), and knowledge units keep one id across versions. Render checks (Lane J, 2026-10-19): a.reading-order (0) and a.rendered-frames (2–5) added; regression rg-12-collapsed-one-frame. a.crossings stays at 1 although the reference measures 0: its two links share a card and can't cross. No frames_fit_screen or links_over_frames_max: no plan mutation makes a frame oversized or a link pass over a third frame here.
